title: 2024.08.06 AQIU Adjudicatory Body decision re Mr. Cius HAI
text:
DECISION OF THE
ADJUDICATORY BODY
As per Article 32.3 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code
Decision by:
Raymond Hack (South Africa), Chairperson
Anna Peniche (Mexico), Member
Alexandre Miguel Mestre (Portugal), Member
In the matter related to:
Mr. James Cius (Haiti), Respondent
Regarding:
Article 5 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code - Duties of good conduct
Article 9 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code - Duty of undivided loyalty
Article 10 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code - Falsification and misuse of
funds
Article 15 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code - Anti-corruption rules
Lausanne, 6 August 2024
* * * * *

I. Overview
1. The present case relates to the conduct of the Executive Director of the
Haitian Federation of the Aquatic Sports (“FHSA”) Mr. James Cius (the
“Respondent” or “Mr. Cius”).
2. More precisely, the Respondent has been charged by the Chief Ethics and
Compliance Officer (the “CECO”) of the Aquatics Integrity Unit (“AQIU”) with
committing a violation of the World Aquatics Integrity Code (“Integrity Code”)
in relation to his involvement in activities in breach of the World Aquatics
regulatory framework, occurred within the FHSA. In this context, a parallel
case has been opened against the FHSA President, Mr. Evenel Mervilus, the
FHSA Treasurer, Mr. Jean Jean Remilus and the FHSA administrator and
adjunct Treasurer, Mrs. Ruby King for similar infringements.
II. Factual background
3. The following summary of the facts does not purport to include every single
contention put forth by the parties during these proceedings. However, the
Adjudicatory Body of the AQIU has thoroughly considered any and all
evidence and arguments submitted, even if no specific or detailed reference
has been made to those arguments in the following outline of its positions
and in the ensuing discussion on the merits.
4. Prior to his provisional suspension, the Respondent was the Executive
Director of the FHSA.
5. In his capacity as Executive Director of the FHSA, the Respondent was
responsible for the management of the FHSA.
6. In 2021, 2022 and 2023, World Aquatics, through the Olympic Aquatics
Support Programme (“OASP”), remitted to the FHSA more than USD
75,000. The purpose of this program was to provide financial support to all
of World Aquatics National Member Federations (“MFs”) in their endeavours
to develop and foster aquatics at all levels within their territories including
covering the athletes' travel expenses.
7. In order to receive the financial support, each MFs had to submit a final
financial report (“OASP Final Financial Report”), documenting all expenses
incurred.
8. By submitting the OASP Final Financial Report, the FHSA committed to
follow the Rules & Regulations of the OASP and certified that the
information provided was a true summary of the expenditure expected to be
associated with the organisation of the projects related to the National
Federation’s OASP.
9. On 16 September 2021, the FHSA submitted the 2021 OASP Final Financial
Report. As proof of the incurred expenses, flight ticket receipts from the
travel agency “Lounair” were attached to the 2021 OASP Final Financial
Report.
10. On 2 August 2022, the FHSA submitted the 2022 OASP Final Financial
Report. As proof of the incurred expenses, flight ticket receipts from the
travel agency “Lounair” were attached to the 2022 OASP Final Financial

Report.
11. For 2023, Mrs. Ruby King as a representative of the FHSA, in line with the
new dispositions of World Aquatics, filed the 2023 OASP Final Report Form.
Also in this case, as proof of the incurred expenses, flight ticket receipts
from the travel agency “Lounair” were attached.
12. On 23 February 2023, the President of the FHSA, Mr. Mervilus signed the
Confirmation Form World Aquatics Support Programme 2023. By signing
this document, Mr. Mervilus committed to follow the World Aquatics Rules
and certified that the projects and objectives were approved by its Board of
Director or equivalent body - which includes the Respondent - and that the
information provided was a true summary of the expenditure expected to be
associated with the organisation of the projects related to the World
Aquatics Support Programme 2023.
III. Procedural background
a. Preliminary procedure before the CECO
13. On 26 January 2024, the President, Mr. Hans Larsen and the Secretary
General, Mr. Patrick Blanchet of the Haitian Olympic Committee lodged a
complaint (the "Complaint") against the FHSA President, Mr. Evenel Mervilus,
the FHSA Treasurer, Mr. Jean Jean Remilus and the FHSA administrator and
adjunct Executive Director, Mrs. Ruby King with World Aquatics - requesting
it to forward it to the AQIU. The object of the Complaint was the financial
mismanagement of the World Aquatics funds granted to the FHSA to cover
athletes’ travel costs for competitions, which were not used as intended or
communicated.
14. On 2 February 2024, the CECO decided to open a preliminary investigation
against the FHSA officials Mr. Mervilus, Mr. Remilus and Mrs. King.
15. In this context, the AQIU questioned and had several exchanges with one of
the mothers of athletes, Mrs. Grand'Pierre, who reported that the FHSA did
not reimburse the athletes' travel expenses and that in an email dated 30
January 2024, the Respondent threatened to exclude her son Alexandre
from competitions after she had concerns about reimbursements.
16. On 6 February 2024, the CECO, pending the outcome of the investigation,
decided to impose a provisional suspension on the Respondent (among
others) given that public confidence in the integrity of the sport of Aquatics
is at risk.
17. The provisional suspension has been effective from 6 February 2024 and
prevents Respondent from participating in any Aquatics-related activity,
including acting as Executive Director of a World Aquatics Member
Federation.
18. On 19 March 2024, the CECO, after being informed of an apology letter that
the Respondent allegedly sent to the parents of the athletes on 6 March
2024, granted an opportunity to give his position on the matter.

b. Main procedure before the CECO
19. On 17 April 2024, considering that he had not received any reply from the
Respondent, the CECO decided to formally charge the Respondent by
means of a notice of charge for possible violations of:
i. Article 5 of the Integrity Code - Duties of good conduct
5.1 Covered Persons must always act honestly, fairly, impartially and in
accordance with the highest ethical standards of integrity and
transparency.
5.2 Covered Persons must avoid any conduct that is inconsistent with
or that undermines in any way the objectives of this Integrity Code.
ii. Article 9 of the Integrity Code - Duty of undivided loyalty
9.9 Covered Persons must not abuse their position within Aquatics in
any way, especially for their own aims or objectives.
iii. Article 10 of the Integrity Code - Falsification and misuse of funds
10.2 Covered Persons must not knowingly give false information,
including false results, nationality and/or date of birth.
10.4 Covered Persons shall not misappropriate or misuse funds,
whether directly or indirectly through, or in conjunction with, third
parties. Covered Persons must use the resources of the World
Aquatics, Continental Organisations or World Aquatics Members only
for lawful and ethical purposes authorised by the relevant body.
iv. Article 15 of the Integrity Code - Anti-corruption Rules
15.1 Each of the following, when committed by a Covered Person
(whether directly or indirectly through any third group), will constitute
an Integrity Code Violation by that Covered Person:
[…]
e) Committing any act not otherwise prohibited under this Integrity
Code that amounts to a violation of any applicable criminal or other law
or regulation where such violation could undermine public confidence
in the integrity of an Event or the sport of Aquatics generally.
20. According to the Notice of Charge, the CECO determined that a ban of 20
years from participating in any Aquatics-related activities on behalf of World
Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or World Aquatics Member,
should be the applicable disciplinary measure in this case.
21. Furthermore, the Respondent was also informed that in accordance with
Article 23.3 of the Integrity Code, he may respond to the Notice of Charge in
one of the following ways:
a. Admit the charge and accept a twenty-year ban from taking part in any
aquatics-related activity;

b. Admit the charge, but dispute and/or seek to mitigate all or any of the
potential consequences and have the Adjudicatory Body determine the
consequences and sanctions; or
c. Deny the charge, and have the Adjudicatory Body determine the
charge and any consequences and sanctions.
22. In his submissions of 18 April 2024, the Respondent admitted the
allegations against him, but disputed and/or sought to mitigate all or any of
the potential consequences.
23. The Respondent admitted that he had made regrettable decisions driven by
wrong intentions during his tenure. He confessed to falsifying documents,
including flight tickets. He justified his actions by explaining that the FHSA
faced financial challenges due to the absence of membership and
participation fees and the lack of financial support from the Haitian Olympic
Committee. In an attempt to obtain additional funds for the FHSA, he
invented expenses and sought contributions from Haitian parents abroad.
He further explained that in his email of 30 January 2024, his main intention
was to address Mrs. Grand'Pierre, as she has a habit of contacting the
Haitian Olympic Committee and the Haitian Ministry of Sport on behalf of the
FHSA without due authorisation. The Respondent then asked for leniency,
stressing his sincere commitment to the progress of swimming in Haiti.
c. Procedure before the Adjudicatory Body
24. On 30 May 2024, the CECO referred the matter to the Adjudicatory Body.
25. On 31 May 2024, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body, afforded Mr. Remilus an
opportunity to provide his position on the matter.
26. In his submissions of 2 June and 5 June 2024, the Respondent admitted
committing a violation for using electronic signatures without the necessary
approval or authorization and he did not expect such a severe sanction for
his actions. He also stated that the main motivation for his infractions, for
which he takes full responsibility, was to ensure the continuation of the
FHSA's activities. He finally requested a second chance and that another
department should review the case to clear Mr. Mervilus, Mr. Remilus and
Mrs. King and reduce the sanction for his actions.
27. On 13 June 2024, the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body clarified that the Panel
has not yet adjudicated the matter and that, according to Article 29 of the
Integrity Code, the Panel feels sufficiently informed and does not consider a
hearing necessary.
IV. CONSIDERATIONS OF THE ADJUDICATORY BODY
A. Jurisdiction, applicability of the Integrity Code and request for a hearing
28. In accordance with Article 24 of the Integrity Code, the Adjudicatory Body of
the AQIU is responsible for adjudicating cases where a respondent has
denied the charges or requests laid by the CECO.
29. The above shows that the AQIU, and, more precisely, the Adjudicatory Body,

has jurisdiction over the case and is entitled to pass a decision on the basis
of the Integrity Code.
30. The Adjudicatory Body took note that the Respondent did not request that a
hearing be held in this matter. In this regard, Article 29.1 of the Integrity Code
clearly states that the Adjudicatory Body has full discretion to decide
whether or not a hearing shall be convened. In this case, as already detailed
in the letter of 13 June 2024 from the Chair of the Adjudicatory Body to the
Respondent, the Adjudicatory Body considers itself sufficiently informed to
render a decision based on the written submissions. In coming to this
conclusion, the Adjudicatory Body noted the fact that the Respondent was
afforded several opportunities to provide his position on this matter by the
CECO and the Adjudicatory Body.
B. Burden and Standard of proof
31. The above having been established, the Adjudicatory Body recalled that, as
a general rule, the AQIU will have the burden of establishing that an Integrity
Code Violation has been committed.
32. The standard of proof will be the balance of probabilities. Facts shall be
established by any reliable means. The Panel shall at its own discretion
determine the admissibility, relevance, materiality and weight of the
evidence offered.
33. The principle of strict liability applies. Therefore, violations are punishable
regardless of whether they have been committed intentionally, recklessly,
and/or negligently.
34. Having clarified the foregoing, the Adjudicatory Body proceeded to consider
the merits of the case.
C. Merits of the case
35. Articles 5.1 and 5.2 of the Integrity Code:
“5.1 Covered Persons must always act honestly, fairly, impartially and in
accordance with the highest ethical standards of integrity and
transparency”.
“5.2 Covered Persons must avoid any conduct that is inconsistent with or
that undermines in any way the objectives of this Integrity Code”.
36. Article 9.9 of the Integrity Code:
“9.9 Covered Persons must not abuse their position within Aquatics in any
way, especially for their own aims or objectives”.
37. Articles 10.2 and 10.04 of the Integrity Code:
“10.2 Covered Persons must not knowingly give false information, including
false results, nationality and/or date of birth”.
“10.4 Covered Persons shall not misappropriate or misuse funds, whether
directly or indirectly through, or in conjunction with, third parties. Covered

Persons must use the resources of the World Aquatics, Continental
Organisations or World Aquatics Members only for lawful and ethical
purposes authorised by the relevant body”.
38. Article 15.1 e) of the Integrity Code:
“15.1 Each of the following, when committed by a Covered Person (whether
directly or indirectly through any third group), will constitute an Integrity
Code Violation by that Covered Person:
e) Committing any act not otherwise prohibited under this Integrity Code
that amounts to a violation of any applicable criminal or other law or
regulation where such violation could undermine public confidence in the
integrity of an Event or the sport of Aquatics generally”.
39. After review of the full case file, the Adjudicatory Body considers it has been
established that the conduct of the Respondent falls under these provisions.
40. Since the Respondent was active as Executive Director within the FHSA, he
falls within the definition of a “Covered Person” under Article 4.1 a) of the
Integrity Code.
41. By producing tampered flight ticket receipts and providing false information
for the purpose of receiving funds from the OASP, the Respondent
committed improper practices, acts of misbehaviours and falsification or
alteration of documents and providing false information within the meaning
of Articles 5.1, 5.2, 9.9, 10.2, 10.4 and 15.1 e) of the Integrity Code.
42. In this regard the Adjudicatory Body considers that the Respondent's
admission is self-evident and adequate to corroborate the violation. Indeed,
the Respondent has candidly confessed to falsifying flight tickets and
pursued personal interests during his tenure.
43. Furthermore, by failing to reimburse the athletes' families for all travel
expenses they incurred for their participation in competitions and
threatening to exclude them from competitions, the Respondent committed
acts of misbehaviours within the meaning of Articles 5.1 and 5.2 of the
Integrity Code.
44. The failure to reimburse the travel expenses has inflicted hardship for the
athletes and their families who had to bear the costs themselves to
participate in competitions, expenses that were supposed to be covered by
the FHSA. Moreover, the actions of the Respondent, such as requesting
reimbursements for non-existent athletes’ flights, further exacerbate the
violations committed and the consequences on the athletes. Such deceitful
practices not only betray the trust of the athletes but also tarnish the
integrity of the FHSA and the governing body responsible for upholding its
principles.
45. Also in this regard, the Adjudicatory Body considers that the Respondent’s
admission, together with the e-mail he sent to Mrs. Grand’Pierre on 30
January 2024, is self-evident and adequate to corroborate the violation.
46. The Respondent justified his actions by explaining that the FHSA faced
financial challenges due to the absence of membership and participation

fees and the lack of financial support from the Haitian Olympic Committee.
In an attempt to obtain additional funds for the FHSA, he invented expenses
and sought contributions from Haitian parents abroad.
47. He further explained that in his email of 30 January 2024, his main intention
was to address Mrs. Grand'Pierre, as she has a habit of contacting the
Haitian Olympic Committee and the Haitian Ministry of Sport on behalf of the
FHSA without due authorisation.
48. The Adjudicatory Body, while acknowledging the commendable admission of
the charges, considers that these arguments are neither a valid reason nor a
justification that could excuse such serious and condemnable behaviour as
tampering with invoices and threatening athletes. In this connection, the
Adjudicatory Body notes that Haitian Olympic Committee stopped subsidies
to the FHSA because it was suspended due to the irresponsible actions of
the FHSA officials.
49. In addition, the Respondent admitted using the electronic signatures of the
FHSA President and of the FHSA Treasurer without their approval, resulting
in the creation of unauthorised documents within the FHSA.
50. In this respect, the Adjudicatory Body notes that this explanation is irrelevant
as well as not credible as the 2021 and 2022 OASP Final Financial Report
and the 2023 Confirmation Form World Aquatics Support Programme were
signed with a handwritten signature and not with an electronic signature.
51. In light of the foregoing, the Adjudicatory Body deems that the Respondent
violated Articles 5.1, 5.2, 9.9, 10.2, 10.4 and 15.1 e) of the Integrity Code.
D. Applicable sanction
52. As per Article 33.1 of the Integrity Code, any one or more of the following
sanctions may be imposed for an Integrity Code Violation:
a) a warning as to future conduct;
b) a reprimand;
c) a fine in an amount proportionate to the seriousness of the violation;
d) an order of reimbursement or restitution;
e) a suspension from carrying out specific activities on behalf of World
Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or World Aquatics Member
for a specified period;
f) a period of ineligibility, the length of which is to be determined based on
what is proportionate in the circumstances of the case, taking into
account in particular (i) the nature of the violation(s), (ii) the degree of fault
of the Covered Person, (iii) the harm that the violation(s) has/have done to
the sport, (iv) the need to deter future violations, and (v) any specific
aggravating or mitigating factors; and
g) any other sanction deemed appropriate, including, but not limited to
disqualification of results, annulment of results of any Event, removal

from office, forfeiture of points and/or of quota places and/or of hosting
rights, other loss of privileges, no contact directives, requirement to
complete educational or other programs, and return of World Aquatics
awards.
53. In this case, after considering (i) the nature of the violations, (ii) the degree of
fault of the Respondent, (iii) the harm that the violations have done to the
sport, (iv) the need to deter future violations and (v) any specific aggravating
or mitigating factors, the Adjudicatory Body has decided to impose a ten-
year suspension against the Respondent from taking part in any Aquatic-
related activities on behalf of World Aquatics and/or Continental
Organisation and/or World Aquatics Member.
54. The Respondent’s repeated violation of the Integrity Code cannot be taken
lightly. The Respondent is an experienced official and a former Executive
Director of a World Aquatics Member.
55. The Respondent further committed the above-described conduct in full
knowledge at the expense of World Aquatics and to the detriment of the
FHSA athletes.
56. As widely demonstrated indeed, the Respondent admitted to having
produced tampered invoices in order to receive the subsidies of the OASP
and also to deny athletes reimbursement for all travel expenses incurred for
their participation in competitions.
57. Therefore, the Respondent’s conduct must be condemned in every way,
especially in view of the position he holds in Aquatics.
58. With respect to the length of the period of ineligibility, the Adjudicatory Body
notes that in a similar case of tampering with invoices in order to request
reimbursements from World Aquatics committed by the former President of
the Chilean Swimming Federation, the Adjudicatory Body imposed a 20-
year suspension on him.1
59. Considering the above, the Adjudicatory Body is convinced that also in this
case it is paramount to issue a significant sanction to prevent such conduct
in the future and impose on the Respondent a suspension for a fixed period
of ten (10) years from taking part in any Aquatic-related activities on behalf
of World Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or World Aquatics
Member.
60. The suspension imposed on the Respondent shall also prevent him from
attending in any capacity, any aquatics International Competition, as defined
at Article 2.2 of the World Aquatics Competition Regulations. For the sake of
clarity, the Olympic Games fall within the definition of International
Competition.
1 https://aquaticsintegrity.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/2024.02.29-Decision-of-the-AQIU-
Adjudicatory-Body-re-Marcos-JARA.pdf
See also: CAS 2019/A/6344 Marco Polo Del Nero v. Fédération Internationale de Football
Association (FIFA) and CAS 2018/A/6072 Kwesi Nyantakyi v. Fédération Internationale de Football
Association (FIFA)

61. Finally, the Adjudicatory Body observes that as per Article 21 of the Integrity
Code, the Respondent is as of 6 February 2024 provisionally suspended on
the ground that public confidence in the integrity of the sport of Aquatics is
at risk.
62. In this regard, the Adjudicatory Body notes that the suspension imposed
should be credited for the months during which the Respondent was
provisionally suspended, thus the ten-year suspension shall be effective
from the date in which the Respondent was provisionally suspended.

V. DECISION OF THE ADJUDICATORY BODY
(i) The AQIU has jurisdiction over this matter.
(ii) The Respondent has violated Articles 5.1, 5.2, 9.9, 10.2, 10.4 and
15.1 e) of the Integrity Code.
(iii) The Respondent is sanctioned with a 10-year period of ineligibility
from taking part in any Aquatic-related activities on behalf of
World Aquatics and/or Continental Organisation and/or World
Aquatics Member and/or recognised body. The sanction begins on
the day in which the Respondent was provisionally suspended, i.e.
6 February 2024.
(iv) This decision is rendered without costs.
(v) As per Article 35 of the World Aquatics Integrity Code, this decision
can be appealed to CAS within twenty-one (21) calendar days of
the appealing Party’s receipt of the written reasoned decision in
question by email.
On behalf of the Panel of the Adjudicatory Body of the Aquatics Integrity Unit:
Anna Peniche Raymond Hack Alexandre Miguel Mestre
Member Chairperson Member
